result: Inhibitory neurons from the interposed nucleus (Int-Vgat) project widely throughout the brainstem beyond the inferior olive, targeting sensory structures (ECU, CU, NTS, SPVi, PB, PSV, vestibular nuclei), motor structures (TRN, PG, RN bilaterally), and cerebellar cortex. These projections are GABAergic as confirmed by Gad65/67 immunopositivity and Slc32a1 expression (98% of labeled cells), and persist even with highly restricted injections to IntA.
evaluation: Claims C4-C48 provide converging evidence from anterograde tracing, immunohistochemistry, and in situ hybridization. The GABAergic phenotype is well-validated (C29-C31), and the widespread projections are documented across multiple injection sites including the most restricted injection (C48). The consistency across methods and specimens strongly supports this major finding.

result: IO-projecting inhibitory neurons (IntIO-Vgat) show more restricted terminations than all Int-Vgat neurons, consistently targeting dorsal PG, PRN, TRN, IO, and vestibular complex. This suggests at least some IO-projecting cells collateralize to a subset of brainstem targets.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 demonstrate that intersectional labeling of IO-projecting Vgat neurons yields a more restricted but still diverse projection pattern. The interpretation (C51) appropriately acknowledges alternative explanations related to methodological constraints. The data support collateralization of at least some IO-projecting inhibitory neurons.

result: Excitatory Int-Ntsr1 neurons project to known targets including brainstem motor structures (PARN, V, RN, SC), vestibular nuclei, pontine nuclei (TRN, PG), thalamus (VM, VAL, CM, PCN, MD, PF, VP, PO), and form nucleocortical mossy fibers. A subset (3/5 animals) showed sparse Vglut2-positive terminals in contralateral IO.
evaluation: Claims C52-C64 provide comprehensive mapping of excitatory projections with immunohistochemical validation (C52-C53) and in situ hybridization. The projection patterns align with prior literature (multiple citations). The sparse glutamatergic IO projection (C63) is a novel observation but appropriately reported as variable across specimens.

result: RN-projecting Ntsr1 neurons (IntRN-Ntsr1) show projection patterns nearly identical to all Int-Ntsr1 neurons, with exceptions being projections to lobule 8, APN, IO, and PPN which were unique to Int-Ntsr1. Terminal fields in contralateral thalamus and spinal cord support collateralization of RN-projecting neurons.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 demonstrate that intersectional labeling recapitulates most Int-Ntsr1 projections, supporting widespread collateralization. The observation aligns with prior work (C67 cites Sathyamurthy et al., 2020). The differences between methods are clearly documented.

result: AAVretro-Cre injections into RN label both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in Int that project to RN, with terminals observed in both IO and RN.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by the AAVretro-Cre experiments showing mixed labeling and terminal immunostaining (referenced in Figure 4—figure supplement 1-2). This provides independent confirmation that both cell types project to RN.

result: Int-Vgat and IntIO-Vgat neurons are significantly smaller (14.4-14.5 μm diameter) than Int-Ntsr1 and IntRN-Ntsr1 neurons (22.1-22.2 μm diameter), with no significant difference within genotype groups (p<0.0001 between genotypes, p>0.99 within genotypes).
evaluation: Claims C69-C73 provide quantitative morphometric data with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's test) and adequate sample sizes (125-404 neurons per group across 4-5 mice). The statistical significance is clearly established.

result: Int-Vgat neurons preferentially target sensory structures while Int-Ntsr1 neurons preferentially target modulatory regions (p=0.001 and p=0.0002 respectively). Within shared targets, the two cell types innervate distinct subregions, and their axons follow different trajectories through the brainstem. Morphologically, Int-Vgat terminals are fine caliber beaded varicosities while Int-Ntsr1 terminals show mossy fiber specializations.
evaluation: Claims C74-C85 provide both quantitative (C74-C76 with statistical tests) and qualitative comparisons. The statistical analyses use appropriate tests (Welch's t-test with FDR correction). The morphological distinctions (C77-C85) are well-documented with imaging. The hemispheric bias trend (C76) is appropriately reported as non-significant after FDR correction.

result: Vglut2-Cre mice show high specificity for glutamatergic neurons (99% Slc17a6+). Rabies tracing from Vglut2-Cre (72.9±9.6% starter cells in Int) and Vgat-Cre (80.8±4.7% in Int) mice labeled Purkinje cells predominantly in ipsilateral Lobules 4/5, Crus 1, and Simplex, with no contralateral PC label.
evaluation: Claims C86-C93 validate the genetic specificity and document PC input patterns. The quantitative data on starter cell locations and PC distributions are clearly reported. The lack of contralateral PC label (C93) is an important negative control.

result: Extracerebellar inputs to Vglut2-Cre and Vgat-Cre Int neurons are diverse and largely shared, with both receiving inputs from motor, sensory, and modulatory regions. No single extracerebellar region accounts for >10% of inputs. A notable exception is LRN, which provides significantly more input to Vgat-Cre neurons (5.9%) than Vglut2-Cre neurons (0.4%, p=0.004).
evaluation: Claims C94-C102 document input patterns with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis. The LRN difference (C100) is statistically significant with clear effect size. The overall similarity of inputs (C98, p=0.2) is appropriately reported. The widespread integration interpretation (C99) is reasonable given the data.

result: Many brainstem regions (ECU, PRN, TRN, PG, LRN) both provide input to and receive projections from Int neurons, forming reciprocal loops. Thalamic nuclei receive projections but do not provide input, while motor/somatosensory cortex and subthalamic nucleus provide input without receiving projections.
evaluation: Claims C103-C105 and C120 integrate anterograde and retrograde tracing data to identify reciprocal connectivity patterns. The observations are clearly documented and extend prior findings (citations provided in C120). The asymmetries in connectivity (C104-C105) are important organizational features.

result: The current findings, combined with prior literature, suggest inhibitory projections from cerebellar nuclei may be more prominent than widely appreciated. Previous studies have documented glycinergic projections from medial nucleus, collateralization to hypothalamus, and some evidence for lateral nucleus inhibitory projections, though the literature has been inconsistent.
evaluation: Claims C106-C111 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior literature. The interpretation (C106) is supported by multiple citations and acknowledges both corroborating and potentially contradictory prior work (C110). The synthesis is balanced and well-supported.

result: The authors propose potential functional roles for inhibitory projections including: modulation of sensory gain for predicted movement consequences, active cancellation of sensory reafference, homeostatic regulation of mossy fiber inputs via pontine nuclei feedback, gating of cortical information for skill learning, and neural integration for gaze/postural control.
evaluation: Claims C112-C115 and C121 are explicitly speculative interpretations (all cite theoretical work but lack direct experimental validation). While the hypotheses are reasonable given the anatomical findings, they remain untested. The authors appropriately frame these as potential roles requiring future investigation.

result: Prior transcriptomic and projection-based studies identified multiple excitatory cell types in IntA, including those targeting brainstem nuclei versus ZI, and spinal-projecting neurons (<20%) that collateralize to MDRNv, RN, and VAL.
evaluation: Claims C116-C119 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations (Kebschull et al., 2020; Sathyamurthy et al., 2020). These provide important context for interpreting the current findings.

result: A few neocortical inputs to intermediate/interstitial CbN groups were observed in rabies tracing experiments.
evaluation: Claim C122 reports a minor observation from the rabies tracing data. While not extensively characterized, it is clearly documented.
